title: Unauthorized machine command
question: What happens when someone tries to change a machine setting they are not allowed to change?
summary: An operator panel on a filling line tries to write a new setpoint into a protected machine namespace. TrailMQ identifies the client, applies the access policy, refuses the command, and keeps an attributable record of the refusal.

actors.description: The operator panel on filling line 07

steps.headline: Machine command blocked
steps.explanation: The connected operator panel is not permitted to write into the protected machine control namespace, so the command never reaches the machine.
steps.technicalNote: The publish is refused at the broker. TrailMQ does not acknowledge it, so the client learns the command did not take effect instead of assuming it did.

steps.headline: The refusal was recorded, with who and why
steps.explanation: The block is not just a dropped message. TrailMQ kept a record naming the client, the identity behind it, the action attempted, the topic, and the reason the policy refused it.
steps.technicalNote: The record carries the decision reason as the broker evaluated it, which is what makes a later review possible without reconstructing intent from raw traffic.

closing.headline: That is the difference
closing.explanation: A conventional broker can also reject this publish. What TrailMQ adds is that the refusal is attributable and reviewable afterwards: the same event is in Activity, with the identity, the topic and the reason attached.
closing.next: Open Activity and filter Outcome: Denied to find this refusal.
